unitDescription.value: In this unit, students investigate how food and fibre enterprises use design and technology to respond to production challenges and changing consumer needs. Students examine a local agricultural industry and identify an opportunity to improve the production, handling, storage, transport or marketing of its products. They develop and evaluate alternative ideas before producing a model or prototype of their preferred solution. Throughout the design process, students consider the needs of producers and customers, as well as safety, ethics, sustainability, cost and commercial viability. The unit develops practical design skills while introducing students to innovation and enterprise within Australia’s agricultural industries.

description.value: In this unit, students investigate authentic challenges within local food and fibre industries, ranging from cattle and poultry management to horticulture and rural mechanisation. Students apply design thinking to develop solutions that improve the production, handling, storage, or marketing of agricultural goods. By focusing on the needs of a specific producer or customer, students explore safety, ethics, and commercial viability while refining their technical production skills. Through the development of a model or prototype and a corresponding commercial proposal, students engage with innovation and enterprise, balancing practical constraints with creative, sustainable design. This unit emphasises the real-world application of design technologies in an agricultural context, preparing students to critically evaluate the lifecycle and impact of their designed solutions.
description.aiNotes:
Students investigate a real problem facing a local agricultural producer and design a solution that improves how food or fibre is produced, handled, stored, transported or marketed.

This would suit country boys because it could involve cattle, fishing, cropping, poultry, horticulture, beekeeping, rural machinery or livestock rather than feeling like another classroom sustainability project.

Possible student projects

Students could design:

a safer livestock-feeding system
a portable animal shelter or shade structure
a better system for transporting produce
an egg-collection or chicken-feeding system
a water-saving trough or irrigation system
a farm-gate produce stall
protective packaging for local produce
a storage system that reduces food spoilage
a device for safely handling livestock
a modular beehive transport or storage solution
a service for connecting local producers with customers
a redesigned product made from wool, timber or another local fibre

They would not all need to make the same product. They could select an agricultural sector, identify a producer or user, and develop a solution suited to that context.

Strong assessment concept
Design brief

Design a product, service or environment that improves an aspect of a food or fibre enterprise. The solution must respond to the needs of a specific producer or customer and consider safety, ethics, sustainability, production costs and commercial viability.

Students would:

Select a food or fibre enterprise.
Investigate how the enterprise currently operates.
Identify a genuine production, handling or marketing problem.
Develop criteria with the producer or user in mind.
Generate and test alternative ideas.
Produce a model, prototype or working product.
Develop a simple commercial proposal.
Evaluate whether the solution is practical and viable.

The commercial proposal could include estimated production cost, sale price, target market, branding and how the design creates value. That brings in the innovation and enterprise emphasis of AC9TDE10K02 without turning the unit into a business subject.

keyTeachingExperiences.value: Students begin by investigating the complex 'Paddock to Product' journey, focusing on local Central Queensland commodities such as beef and pineapples. Through collaborative mapping, they trace the supply chain from primary production through to processing, transport, and retail, identifying where value is added and where inefficiencies occur. Explicit teaching focuses on the integration of technology in modern farming systems, highlighting how digital and mechanical innovations address global challenges in resource efficiency and food security. Students conclude the week by categorising specific production challenges related to pest management and post-harvest handling within a chosen agricultural sector.

resources.value: Meat & Livestock Australia (MLA) industry reports, AgriFutures Australia case studies, supply chain mapping software (Lucidchart or Canva), local agricultural commodity data (e.g., Livingstone Shire agricultural profiles).

theory.value: Examination of the food and fibre production context, focusing on the interconnected nature of modern agricultural supply chains. Students investigate the role of emerging technologies, such as GPS-guided machinery, automated irrigation systems, and remote sensing, in improving sustainability and yield. Theoretical focus is placed on 'Life Cycle Thinking' and how technological interventions can mitigate environmental impacts during the production and transport phases. Students learn to identify specific constraints within the agricultural industry, including biosecurity protocols, climate variability, and ethical considerations in animal welfare or chemical use.

prac.value: Students conduct a supply chain mapping workshop, using digital tools to visualise the movement of a local agricultural product from the farm gate to the consumer. They participate in a 'Tech Audit' of current agricultural equipment, evaluating the effectiveness of existing tools versus automated alternatives. Practical activities include simulated post-harvest handling scenarios where students must identify points of potential product degradation and propose technology-based monitoring solutions, such as temperature sensors or moisture-controlled storage models.

assessment.value: Formative: Completion of a detailed supply chain flowchart and a summary report identifying three major technological gaps in a local agricultural industry.

activities.title: Deconstructing the Five-Stage Ag Supply Chain
activities.teacherDoes: Explicitly model the five foundational stages of agricultural supply chains: Primary Production, Processing, Storage/Cold Chain, Transport/Distribution, and Retail/Consumer. Using the example of Central Queensland beef production, write the stage labels on the board while verbally contrasting 'value-adding' (e.g., grading, packaging) with 'points of loss' (e.g., transport shrinkage, spoilage). Provide a worked example: 'If we are at the Primary Production stage, the output is live cattle; the input is feed and water. At Processing, the output becomes boxed beef, adding value through quality control.'
activities.studentsDo: Observe the modelled flow. Complete the flow diagram in the workbook by identifying the five stages and defining one specific 'input' and one 'output' for the Beef Cattle supply chain journey.
activities.visibleInstructions: Complete the five-stage supply chain flow in your workbook. For each stage, identify one primary input (what goes in) and one output (what comes out) related to the Central Queensland beef industry.
activities.questioning:
question: Why is cold-chain storage critical immediately following processing?
expected: To prevent microbial growth, adhere to food safety regulations, and maintain the chemical integrity of the meat before transport.
question: In what way does the transport stage influence the economic value of the final product?
expected: Transport incurs costs and logistical risks such as bruising or weight loss (shrinkage), which decreases value; however, it is essential to reach high-demand export or domestic retail markets.
activities.scaffolding: Supply Chain Stages: 1. Primary Production (farm/station): Input: pasture/fodder; Output: live cattle. 2. Processing (abattoir): Input: live cattle; Output: primal cuts/packaged beef. 3. Cold Storage (chilling/preservation): Input: packaged beef; Output: temperature-controlled inventory. 4. Distribution/Logistics (freight/tracking): Input: palletised meat; Output: delivery to wholesaler. 5. Retail/Consumer (butcher/supermarket/export): Input: beef inventory; Output: consumer purchase.
activities.eLearning: Project the interactive flow diagram on the main screen to mirror the workbook layout. Use the 'call to action website buttons convert visitors' search terms to prompt a brief discussion on how digital interfaces for tracking (like QR codes on meat packaging) function as a modern supply chain input.

activities.title: AgTech Terminology & Core Concepts
activities.teacherDoes: Explicitly define key AgTech concepts: Precision Agriculture, Remote Sensing, Telemetry, and Autonomous Guidance. Connect these to regional Central Queensland challenges, such as the scale of broadacre grazing properties and the need for fuel efficiency in cattle operations. Model the matching process by selecting one term (e.g., 'Telemetry') and identifying how the 'automated transmission of data' fits the description of transmitting water level data from remote bores to a homestead dashboard.

activities.visibleInstructions: Match each AgTech term in the left column with its correct definition from the definition bank.
activities.questioning:
question: What does NDVI remote sensing measure in the context of pasture management?
expected: It measures the difference between near-infrared and red light reflectance to quantify plant photosynthetic vigour, allowing producers to identify high-biomass grazing areas.
question: Why is telemetry technology particularly critical for large-scale grazing stations in Central Queensland?
expected: It transmits data like water tank levels or soil moisture over vast distances, eliminating the significant labour and fuel costs associated with daily manual bore runs.
activities.scaffolding: Precision Agriculture: A management strategy using data to target inputs (fertiliser, water, chemicals) with high spatial accuracy to maximise yield and reduce waste. Remote Sensing: Acquiring information about crops, soil, or vegetation from satellite, aircraft, or drone sensors without physical contact. Telemetry: Automated recording and transmission of sensor data (e.g., tank levels, flow meters) from remote sites to a central device. Autonomous Guidance: Driverless machine operation using GNSS/GPS positioning for automated path planning and navigation.
activities.eLearning: Display high-resolution satellite imagery showing NDVI pasture variation and a diagram of a telemetry system transmitting data from remote water troughs to a farm office.
activities.transition: Now that we have established our AgTech vocabulary, we will apply these concepts to examine how these technologies improve specific sustainability metrics in our local supply chains.

orientate.smartStart: What are the three most common environmental factors that cause fresh fruit or meat to degrade during storage and transit?
orientate.learningGoalDisplay: I can identify points of post-harvest product degradation and specify sensor technologies to monitor produce quality

activities.title: Deconstructing Post-Harvest Degradation Factors
activities.teacherDoes: Explicitly define the critical environmental variables impacting post-harvest quality: temperature (microbial growth), humidity (moisture loss/wilting), mechanical shock (internal bruising/seal failure), and ethylene accumulation (ripening control). Model the selection of sensor payloads by demonstrating how a digital thermistor is chosen for cold-chain monitoring whereas an accelerometer is essential for logistics audit. Provide an example: 'When monitoring beef transit, temperature alone is insufficient; vibration monitoring using a 3-axis accelerometer is critical to prevent micro-fissures in vacuum-sealed packaging.'
activities.studentsDo: Record the four degradation variables in the workbook. Complete the sensor-matching table by selecting the correct monitoring technology for each environmental factor from the provided bank.
activities.visibleInstructions: Using the provided bank of definitions, match the appropriate sensor technology to the environmental degradation factor listed in the table.
activities.questioning:
question: Why does excessive humidity cause issues in cold storage even when the temperature is maintained?
expected: Condensation occurs, leading to fungal pathogen proliferation and mould growth on the surface of fresh produce.
question: What is the primary function of an accelerometer sensor during the transport of fragile horticultural commodities?
expected: To quantify mechanical shock and road vibration, which correlates to physical bruising or packaging integrity failures.
activities.scaffolding:
Definitions for Sensor Types:
1. Digital Thermistor: Resistive element that varies resistance based on temperature; used for cold-chain continuity.
2. Capacitive Hygrometer: Measures dielectric changes to determine relative humidity levels.
3. 3-axis Accelerometer: Detects changes in G-force and mechanical acceleration in X, Y, and Z planes.
4. Electrochemical/NDIR Sensor: Detects gas concentrations, specifically ethylene, via gas diffusion or infrared absorption.
activities.eLearning: Display sensor specification data sheets on the board. Search YouTube for: 'call to action website convert visitors' to understand technical data thresholds for supply chain interventions.

activities.questioning: If the temperature probe registers 16°C inside the refrigerated container for over two hours, what automated action should the telematics unit take? Expected: Send an immediate SMS/email alert to the driver and fleet manager and trigger an automated cooling diagnostic. activities.title: Classifying Design Criteria Matrix
activities.teacherDoes: Explicitly teach how professional designers categorise constraints across the three pillars of project feasibility: WHS & Safety Standards, Environmental Sustainability, and Commercial Viability. Demonstrate how a single criterion—such as 'hot-dip galvanised structural steel'—influences multiple pillars: Safety (prevents sudden structural failure under animal impact), Sustainability (maximises lifecycle before replacement), and Commercial Viability (minimises lifetime depreciation and maintenance costs). Expected: Australian workplace health and safety legislation makes safety compliance legally mandatory; non-compliant agricultural tools cannot be sold or operated commercially.
How does selecting recycled polymer for paddock feed troughs support both sustainability and commercial viability?
Expected: It diverts plastic waste from landfill while providing superior resistance to chemical rot and animal impact, directly reducing long-term replacement expenses.

activities.scaffolding:

- Put to another use: Deploy an existing tool in an entirely different operational context.
- Eliminate: Remove non-essential parts to reduce friction, cost, or points of mechanical failure.
- Reverse: Invert the operating sequence, physical orientation, or flow of livestock/produce.

activities.title: Defining the Triple Bottom Line
activities.teacherDoes: Introduce the Triple Bottom Line (TBL) as the standard framework for evaluating design viability in industry. Model the analysis: 'When we select a material for our AgTech prototype, we do not just look at the price tag (Economic). What if a material is cheap but has high environmental impact? Expected: It may lower immediate production costs but increase total lifecycle costs due to disposal fees or reduced community acceptance.

activities.teacherDoes: Explicitly teach the concept of 'Critical Path' in fabrication, using the St Brendan's workshop environment as a context. Model how a dependency error (e.g., 'assembling before measuring') causes project failure. Example: 'If we assemble before verifying dimensions, we risk material wastage. question: How does identifying the critical path help manage project risk?
expected: Expected: It identifies the tasks that must be completed on time to prevent the overall project deadline from slipping.
question: Why is it inefficient to overlap the 'Assemble' and 'Procure' stages?
expected: Expected: Procuring after assembly starts leads to idle labour and stop-start workflow, increasing potential for material waste and budget blowout.

lessons.title: Technical Drawing Standards: Orthogonal and Sectional Views
lessons.learningGoal: Construct orthogonal and sectional technical drawings compliant with AS 1100 standards to communicate internal and external mechanical components.

activities.title: AS 1100 Orthogonal Projection Conventions
activities.teacherDoes: Model third-angle orthogonal projection on the whiteboard using an AgTech sensor bracket. Demonstrate how the front, top, and right-side views project along parallel construction lines. Contrast visible outlines (0.5 mm continuous line) with hidden detail (0.3 mm dashed line) and cutting planes (thick line with directional arrows labeled A-A). Model how perspective distorts dimensions whereas orthogonal projection maintains a strict 1:1 or 1:2 scale for manufacturing precision.
activities.studentsDo: Follow the teacher demonstration of the glass box projection method. Complete the AS 1100 drawing convention match table in the workbook by matching each term to its correct definition from the bank.
activities.visibleInstructions: Match each drawing convention term in the left column with its corresponding AS 1100 definition from the bank.
activities.questioning:
question: Why is orthogonal projection mandatory for manufacturing compared to an isometric or perspective sketch?
expected: Orthogonal views show the true shape, geometry, and unforeshortened dimensions required for CNC milling or manual fabrication.
question: Why must hidden detail lines remain dashed and thinner than visible outlines?
expected: To prevent visual confusion between exterior solid faces and internal cavities or drill holes.
activities.scaffolding: Definitions: 1. Third-Angle Orthogonal Projection: A multiview method where views are projected onto planes situated between the observer and the object. 2. Hidden Detail Line: A thin, evenly spaced dashed line (0.3 mm) showing obscured features. 3. Cutting Plane: A heavy dashed or chain line with arrows indicating the line and direction of a sectional cut. 4. Sectional Hatching: Uniform thin lines drawn at 45 degrees to indicate solid cut material.
activities.eLearning: Laptops closed and eyes on the front board while projection standards are demonstrated.
activities.transition: Pre-warn students that we will now co-construct a sectional view of an AgTech solenoid valve casing.

bank: Standard 2D multiview layout where the top view sits above the front view and right view sits on the right.
Thin dashed line indicating interior surfaces or edges not visible from the current exterior angle.
Thick stepped or straight line with directional arrows marking where a component is sliced open.
Uniform thin parallel lines angled at 45 degrees indicating solid material sliced by a cutting plane.

activities.teacherAnswerKey:
Third-Angle Projection: Standard 2D multiview layout where the top view sits above the front view and right view sits on the right.
Hidden Detail Line: Thin dashed line indicating interior surfaces or edges not visible from the current exterior angle.
Cutting Plane Line: Thick stepped or straight line with directional arrows marking where a component is sliced open.
Section Hatching: Uniform thin parallel lines angled at 45 degrees indicating solid material sliced by a cutting plane.

activities.title: Guided Sectional Drafting: Solenoid Housing
activities.teacherDoes: Project an isometric view of a cylindrical solenoid valve housing with a stepped cutting plane A-A. Guide the class step-by-step: 1. Identify the central fluid bore and the mounting screw counterbores. 2. Project exterior boundaries onto the drafting grid. 3. Mark hollow channels versus solid metal walls. 4. Apply 45-degree cross-hatch lines strictly across the solid wall sections, leaving the central cavity and fastener holes completely blank. Emphasise that fasteners and open voids must never be hatched. Model the correct line weight ratio: thick continuous lines for visible outlines (Type B) and thin continuous lines (Type H) spaced 2-3 mm apart for hatching.
activities.studentsDo: Follow the teacher's steps to complete the Section A-A cross-sectional drawing on the workbook grid, applying 45-degree hatching strictly to solid wall material and labeling the section title.
activities.visibleInstructions:
1. Draft the exterior profile of the solenoid housing using the cutting plane A-A guide.
2. Leave the internal conduit and fastener voids unshaded.
3. Apply uniform 45-degree hatching across all solid sliced walls.
4. Title the completed view 'Section A-A'.
activities.questioning:
question: If the cutting plane passes directly through a hollow water conduit, why do we leave that region unhatched?
Expected: Hatching represents solid material that has been physically severed by the cutting plane; hollow voids contain no material to hatch.
question: Why are shafts, bolts, and solid webs typically not cross-hatched when cut longitudinally?
Expected: Standard AS 1100 conventions exempt solid cylindrical fasteners to maintain drawing readability and avoid false impressions of internal voids.
activities.scaffolding: Sectional Drafting Rules: 1. Hatch lines must be thin, parallel, and angled at 45 degrees spaced ~2-3 mm apart. 2. Voids, bores, and hollow conduits remain unhatched white space. 3. Boundary lines between solid material and voids must be drawn with solid thick lines (0.5 mm).
activities.eLearning: Monitor students from the rear of the room to verify that drafting set squares are held securely at 45 degrees.

activities.title: Mechanical Assembly Sequencing and Motion Paths
activities.teacherDoes:
Demonstrate the construction of an exploded assembly drawing using a farm gate latch mechanism. Model the fundamental rule of the 'primary datum': identifying the base structural component that remains stationary, and projecting all sub-components outwards along a single, continuous axial centreline (chain line). Illustrate why components must never overlap in an exploded view and how dashed trajectory lines communicate the direction and order of insertion.

Modelled Example:
1. Baseplate (Datum) anchored at origin (0,0).
2. Internal sensor housing aligned to vertical axis.
3. O-ring seal positioned along the linear trajectory.
4. M6 securing fasteners locked into threaded inserts.
activities.studentsDo: Observe the teacher's demonstration on the main projector. Complete the assembly sequence flow in the workbook by ordering the four phases of mechanical prototype assembly from foundational baseplate to final fastener securing.
activities.visibleInstructions: Complete the assembly sequence flow by recording the four stages of mechanical assembly from foundational baseplate to final fastener securing.
activities.questioning:
q: Why must all exploded components share a common axial construction line?
Expected: To clearly show the path of travel and mating surfaces so the fabricator knows exactly which hole or bore each component enters.
q: What occurs if components overlap each other in an exploded view?
Expected: It obscures geometry and fastener alignment, creating ambiguity during physical fabrication.
activities.scaffolding:
Exploded View Principles:
1. Datum Base: The core component that anchors the assembly.
2. Axis of Assembly: A continuous centreline along which parts separate.
3. Trajectory Lines: Thin dashed lines indicating the travel path.
4. Exploded Spacing: Sufficient clearance between parts so no profiles intersect.

activities.title: Hierarchy of Hazard Control Terminology
activities.teacherDoes: Explicitly teach the WHS Hierarchy of Hazard Control mandated in Queensland manufacturing environments. Model how to evaluate a prototype cutting operation using all five tiers: Elimination (purchase pre-cut extrusions), Substitution (use hand shears instead of an angle grinder), Engineering (install blade guards and dust extraction), Administrative (complete workshop induction and post safety signage), and PPE (wear safety glasses and leather riggers gloves). Highlight why PPE is legally regarded as the least reliable control.
activities.studentsDo: Define the key WHS terms by completing the matching table in the workbook, pairing each level of control with its formal industrial definition from the bank.
activities.visibleInstructions: Match each level of the Hierarchy of Hazard Control with its legal WHS definition using the provided definition bank.
activities.questioning: Why does Workplace Health and Safety legislation classify PPE as the least effective control method? Expected: PPE relies entirely on human compliance, correct fitting, and maintenance; if the worker removes or damages the PPE, the hazard remains completely unmitigated. If a technician installs an interlock switch on a CNC router enclosure, which control level has been applied? Expected: An engineering control, because it isolates the moving cutting tool mechanically without relying on user behaviour.
activities.scaffolding:
Hierarchy Definitions: 
- Elimination: Completely remove the hazard or hazardous process from the worksite.
- Substitution: Replace the hazard with a lower-risk tool, chemical, or procedure.
- Engineering Controls: Modify equipment, install physical guards, or isolate the hazard.
- Administrative Controls: Implement training, standard operating procedures, and warning signs.
- Personal Protective Equipment (PPE): Gear worn by the operator to reduce injury severity.
activities.eLearning: Display WorkSafe Queensland Hierarchy of Control pyramid on the classroom projector.
activities.transition: Guide students to apply these control tiers to a structured risk assessment matrix for prototype manufacturing.

Demonstrate how to calculate initial Risk Score (Consequence x Likelihood), establish a multi-tiered control strategy combining Engineering and PPE, and recalculate the Residual Risk to ensure fabrication can proceed safely.

activities.questioning: What is the difference between a hazard and a risk in a workshop environment? Expected: A hazard is anything with the potential to cause harm (e.g., spinning drill bit), while risk is the likelihood and severity of harm occurring under specific operational conditions. Why must a risk assessment be completed before any materials or machinery are touched in the workshop? Expected: To identify and control potential points of failure before physical exposure, fulfilling legal safety requirements and preventing severe workplace injury.
activities.scaffolding:
Risk Matrix Guide:
- High Risk: Potential for permanent injury or amputation (e.g., exposed rotating blades, mains voltage).
- Medium Risk: Minor cuts, burns, or particle eye irritations requiring first aid.
- Low Risk: Minor pinch points or surface abrasions.
Control Formulation: Always pair an Engineering/Administrative control with appropriate PPE.

activities.title: Safe Work Procedure (SWP) Construction
activities.teacherDoes: Explain that a Safe Work Procedure (SWP) is a formal, legally binding standard operating procedure in industry. Model how to structure an SWP across three operational phases: Pre-Operational Checks (guard inspection, emergency stop testing, PPE check), Operational Safety (feed rate, holding technique, exclusion zones), and Post-Operational Shutdown (isolation, debris clearing with brush, tool return). Highlight that brooms and bench brushes must be used to clear metal filings—never bare hands. For example, when drafting a pedestal drill SWP, explicitly state: 'Phase 1: Inspect chuck guard; confirm emergency stop disengages motor; verify AS/NZS 1337 safety glasses donned.'
activities.studentsDo: Draft a detailed Safe Work Procedure for your primary prototype manufacturing tool in the workbook, structuring instructions into Pre-Operational, Operational, and Post-Operational sections.
activities.visibleInstructions:
1. Write the title of your selected machinery or fabrication tool.
2. Detail the pre-start safety checks including emergency stop inspection.
3. Write the operational procedure detailing safe handling and hazard controls.
4. Write the shutdown and workspace clean-up requirements.
activities.questioning:
q: Why are pre-operational checks critical before turning on power to any workshop machine?
expected: To confirm that safety guards are locked, the emergency stop functions correctly, and no tooling or swarf remains jammed in the mechanism.
q: Why must metal swarf or acrylic shavings never be wiped away with bare hands or blown away with compressed air?
expected: Swarf has razor-sharp burrs that cause deep lacerations, and compressed air launches high-velocity projectiles that risk blinding nearby operators.
activities.scaffolding:
SWP Structure:
1. Pre-Operational: Inspect power lead, verify guards in position, fit AS-approved eye protection, test E-stop.
2. Operational: Secure material in vice, maintain 50 mm hand exclusion zone, never leave running machine unattended.
3. Post-Operational: Isolate power at wall switch, wait for spindle to stop completely, sweep swarf using bench brush.

activities.title: Core Prototyping Concepts
activities.teacherDoes: Explicitly explain that functional testing validates sub-assemblies before full integration. Contrast linear manufacturing with iterative design ('build-test-adjust'). Define 'Functional Testing', 'Iterative Design', 'Alpha Testing', and 'Troubleshooting'. Demonstrate on the board how an isolated sensor circuit test prevents hidden wiring faults in a sealed chassis. For example, when testing an agricultural soil moisture sensor, verify the voltage output separately before soldering it to the microcontroller.
activities.studentsDo: Complete the cloze passage in the workbook by selecting the correct technical terms from the word bank to define iterative development.
activities.visibleInstructions: Use the word bank to complete the definitions of functional testing and iterative design in your workbook.
activities.questioning:
question: Why is testing an isolated sensor module more efficient than testing the fully assembled unit?
expected: It isolates failure points and prevents complex multi-variable diagnostics when parts are interconnected.
question: How does iterative design produce superior agricultural tools compared to single-cycle builds?
expected: It incorporates real testing data into mechanical refinements, addressing field durability and assembly tolerances systematically.
activities.scaffolding:
Definitions:
- Functional Testing: Validating that an isolated sub-assembly performs its specified technical task.
- Iterative Design: A cyclic development methodology where prototypes are repeatedly tested and refined based on empirical data.
- Alpha Testing: Preliminary in-house functional trials to identify fundamental design flaws.
- Troubleshooting: The systematic process of diagnosing and correcting mechanical or electronic faults.

activities.title: The Build-Test-Adjust Loop
activities.teacherDoes: Model the decision-making architecture of the 'Build-Test-Adjust' cycle on the board. Emphasise the decision gate: 'Performance criteria met?'. Demonstrate how a 'No' output redirects the engineer to 'Diagnose and Modify Design' before refabrication, whereas a 'Yes' advances the sub-assembly to 'System Integration'. Example script: 'Notice how a failure at the decision gate does not mean starting over completely; it requires targeted diagnostics to refine our specific AgTech sensor housing before moving to integration.'

question: What engineering risk occurs if a prototype bypasses the 'Modify Design' feedback loop after a failed test?
expected: Compounding defects will cause total system failure during full integration.
question: Why is documenting the 'No' path critical for your engineering assessment journal?
expected: It provides empirical evidence of troubleshooting, testing analysis, and design refinement required by QCAA standards.
activities.scaffolding:
Iterative Logic Stages:
1. Fabricate Component (Initial construction based on technical drawings)
2. Perform Alpha Test (Measure against quantifiable success criteria)
3. Decision Gate (Are criteria met? Yes/No)
4. Modify Design (Troubleshoot and adjust if No)
5. Proceed to Integration (Combine sub-assemblies if Yes)

activities.title: Component Functional Audit
activities.teacherDoes: Model how to define quantitative testing metrics for physical and electronic AgTech components. Contrast a vague test ('see if it holds') with a measurable metric ('deflection under 500g static load < 2mm'). Guide students to formulate testable metrics for three discrete components of their design, ensuring they understand the application of tolerances and units of measurement in engineering contexts.
activities.studentsDo: Complete the component audit table in the workbook by naming three distinct components of their prototype, specifying their function, and stating an objective testing metric with numerical tolerances.
activities.visibleInstructions: Audit three core components of your AgTech prototype. Define the function and a measurable testing metric (with units and tolerances) for each in the table below.
activities.questioning: Why is 'it works' invalid as an engineering testing metric? Expected: It is qualitative, subjective, and fails to establish clear failure boundaries. What units of measurement apply to structural joint stability versus an optical or moisture sensor? Expected: Structural joints require millimetres of deflection or kilograms of load; sensors require voltage, resistance, or digital output readings.
activities.scaffolding:
Quantitative Metrics Reference:
- Electronic sensors: Baseline digital reading stability (±5% tolerance) or analog voltage range (0–5V).
- Structural chassis: Deflection under load (<2mm under 500g) or joint squareness (90° ± 0.5°).
- Actuators/mechanisms: Sweep angle (0–180°), rotational speed (RPM), or response time (ms).

activities.title: Diagnostic Root-Cause Analysis
activities.teacherDoes: Demonstrate systematic troubleshooting using a faulty AgTech sub-assembly (e.g., an automated gate latch with excessive hinge play). Model the '5-Whys' diagnostic method: 1. Symptom (gate does not latch), 2. Immediate cause (misaligned strike plate), 3. Root cause (bracket flexed under load due to thin gauge material), 4. Modification (add triangulated gusset brace). Emphasise documenting modifications against design constraints.
activities.studentsDo: Examine their prototype components. Conduct a root-cause analysis on two distinct faults or performance limitations and record them in the Component Troubleshooting Log workbook table.

activities.questioning:
prompt: Why must engineers distinguish between an immediate symptom and a root cause during troubleshooting?
expected: Fixing only the symptom leads to recurring failure under operational stress, while addressing the root cause resolves the underlying design flaw.
prompt: What happens to the prototype's mass or cost constraints if we solve structural flex by simply adding heavier materials?
expected: It may breach total weight, balance, or budget constraints established in the Bill of Materials.
activities.scaffolding:
Root Cause Diagnostic Framework:
- Observed Failure (Symptom): What visible failure occurred during testing? (e.g., joint cracked, sensor reading dropped).
- Root Cause Analysis (Why): What underlying physical condition caused it? (e.g., inadequate bond area, mechanical shear stress, loose wire header).
- Proposed Modification: What specific technical modification will resolve the root cause? (e.g., add gusset plate, increase fastener gauge, solder direct pin joint).

keyTeachingExperiences.value: Students move into the refinement phase of their AgTech prototypes, focusing on technical precision and aesthetic finish to ensure the model is industry-ready. Explicit teaching focuses on Life Cycle Assessment (LCA), where students evaluate the environmental and ethical footprint of their solution from raw material extraction to end-of-life disposal. They begin drafting the commercial proposal, specifically addressing how their technology integrates into existing agricultural workflows while meeting sustainability benchmarks. These lessons bridge the gap between a functional prototype and a commercially viable product, requiring students to justify their material choices through the lens of social and environmental responsibility.

Why must an AgTech designer evaluate raw material extraction when designing hardware for Capricorn Coast farms? Expected: Because embodied energy, transport logistics, and habitat disruption at extraction contribute heavily to the overall carbon debt before the device is even turned on.
How does end-of-life planning influence whether rural hardware contributes to hazardous e-waste or circular manufacturing? Expected: Choosing modular, non-toxic, and recyclable components ensures the hardware can be recovered rather than abandoned in farm landfills.
activities.scaffolding:
Raw Material Extraction: Harvesting or mining virgin natural resources (e.g. bauxite, crude oil) to produce engineering base stock.
Manufacturing: Industrial fabrication, shaping, and assembly of raw stock into functional components.
Use: Operational life on-farm, including maintenance, power consumption, and environmental exposure.
End-of-Life: Decommissioning phase encompassing disposal, disassembly, recycling, or material reclamation.
